default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t1-p1.vietnamese:
This is a notice from the police.

Notice from the police

Recently, damage caused by suspicious phone calls and emails has been increasing throughout the country.

Criminals pretend to be police officers or bank employees in order to deceive people and take their money.

Do not think, “I alone will not be deceived.” No matter who the caller claims to be, remember never to reveal your credit-card or bank-account information.

If you receive an unfamiliar call, remain calm and deal with it carefully.

In elementary schools in Japan, the school usually provides lunch.

The menu is decided each month by a teacher in charge of nutrition and is designed to provide at least one-third of the nutrients children need each day.

However, because meals at home tend to contain a lot of salt, the amount of salt in school lunches is instead prepared so that it does not exceed one-third of the daily requirement.

By skillfully adjusting the seasonings, the dishes are still prepared so that children do not feel that they lack saltiness.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t11-p1.vietnamese:
Studying history is very important.

By learning what happened in the past, why it happened, and how people at the time thought, we can understand the meaning of events happening in the present and predict what may happen in the future.

At that time, it is important not only to think on your own, but also to exchange opinions with your classmates so that you can learn how other people think.

By doing so, we can consider events from many different perspectives and notice things we had never seen before.

This way of learning will be very useful after entering society, so it is better to practice and develop it from a young age.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t12-p1.vietnamese:
This notice is posted in front of a store.

Store Closing Notice

Kobayashi Store has been in business in this shopping district for 50 years.

However, because the owner has reached an age at which it is difficult to continue operating the store, we have decided to close at the end of next month.

There were many times when we thought we might not be able to continue operating, such as during economic downturns and the rise of large department stores.

Nevertheless, thanks to all of you, we have been able to continue operating for 50 years. We would like to express our deepest gratitude.

Although this may come as a sudden announcement, we sincerely thank you for your support over the past 50 years.

Notice Regarding Construction

August 31, 2020

To all residents of Kobayashi Apartments: Due to water-pipe construction, the water supply to our apartment building will be shut off from 10:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on Wednesday, September 10.

Therefore, during this period, you will not be able to use washing machines, showers, or toilets.

However, you may use the public toilet on the first floor.

For inquiries regarding the construction, please contact us at the email address below.

Email address: 1234@kobayashi.jp

We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience and ask for your understanding and cooperation.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t14-p1.vietnamese:
In the past, it was taken for granted that becoming a sushi chef would take more than 10 years.

When I began my training, the instruction from my seniors was extremely strict.

However, if we impose on today’s young chefs the same strict training that we received in the past, they will not be able to endure it and will quit immediately.

If we continue complaining, “Why are young people today so weak?”, the number of people who want to become sushi chefs will continue to decline.

Sushi is a culture that represents Japan.

To preserve that culture in the future, we must devise teaching methods suited to young people in today’s society.

Before going to work or school, many people can often be seen stopping at breakfast shops and eating breakfast there.

In other countries, shops specializing in breakfast are uncommon, and eating at home is the more common habit.

However, recently many people have been living busy lives.

Because these shops save people time preparing breakfast and offer a wide variety of dishes, Taiwan’s breakfast shops are reportedly beginning to gain popularity overseas.

Since it was October and I wanted to do something that felt truly autumnal, I invited a coworker the other day to view the autumn leaves in a nearby park.

However, even though it was already late October, surprisingly, the maple leaves were still green.

This was the first time I had ever experienced anything like it.

Until last year, we could feel the four seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—every three months, but this year, hot days have continued as if summer had grown longer.

Could this also be related to global warming?

Being able to experience the four seasons is one of Japan's beautiful features, so it would be truly regrettable if we could no longer experience them.

It is said that modern people use their eyes too much.

When we look at electronic devices such as computers, smartphones, and televisions for long periods, our eyes gradually become tired without us even realizing it.

Our eyes may begin to feel heavy, or we may gradually lose the ability to see things clearly.

In addition, various other symptoms may appear, such as twitching eyes, and our eyesight may continue to worsen.

To prevent this deterioration, let your eyes rest for about 10 minutes after every hour.

Even simply massaging them or closing your eyes can be effective.

Take time to relieve your eyes of their fatigue.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t25-p1.vietnamese:
Tea-drinking culture can be found all over the world.

Many people add sugar or milk to tea to make it more enjoyable to drink.

Of course, there are countries such as Japan where people do not add sugar to tea. However, viewed globally, there are more countries where sugar is added. In particular, tea in India and Southeast Asian countries is so sweet that Japanese people find it unusually sugary.

Why, then, do people in India and Southeast Asia add so much sugar to tea?

The main reason is that they consider tea a bitter drink, much like coffee.

Moreover, for people living in regions that are hot all year round, sweetness apparently stimulates the appetite and helps soothe bodies fatigued by the heat.

For this reason, they add a very generous amount of sugar.

This is slightly off topic, but the fact that many dishes in India and Southeast Asia are spicy or sour also stems from the same reason.

Their way of thinking about tea is completely different from that of Japanese people, who drink tea to enjoy its original flavor.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t26-p1.outline.1.labe: The real reason life becomes boring
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t26-p1.outline.1.note: The author explains that the cause is their own dulled sensitivity and reduced concern after gaining extensive experience, not the surrounding circumstances. Provides the basis for Question 1.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t26-p1.outline.2.labe: The nature of what makes life interesting
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t26-p1.outline.2.note: The author shifts to the assertion that something interesting is always nearby and must be discovered personally; the demonstrative 「それ」 in Question 2 refers to this truth.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t26-p1.outline.3.labe: Specific actions for discovering something new
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t26-p1.outline.3.note: Suggests concrete actions: change small habits, such as taking a different route to work or leaving earlier, to discover something new. Evidence for Question 3.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t26-p1.vietnamese:
How many surprises fill your everyday life, and how many interesting things surround you?

Many people complain, "Every day, I repeat the same things, so life is boring. When I was a child, the day seemed to pass much faster than it does now."

The reason your present life feels ordinary and boring may simply be that your own ability to notice things has become less sensitive.

It is absolutely not because of your surroundings.

As people grow older and gain more experience, they tend to feel that they know everything, and they gradually become less interested in the things around them.

However, surprisingly interesting things exist very close to you.

Interesting things are not something someone brings to you; they are something you must discover for yourself.

You simply have not noticed them yet.

If you try going to work by a different route or leave home a little earlier than usual, you may make surprising new discoveries.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t27-p1.outline.1.note: Modern businesses make fewer durable products and prefer items that wear out quickly so customers must buy them repeatedly; the author criticizes this mindset.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t27-p1.vietnamese:
One day, my wife said this:

“I bought these three pairs of socks at a store in Kyoto ten years ago for 1,000 yen, and I can still wear them. They were all handmade by craftspeople. Japanese craftsmanship is amazing, isn’t it?”

Nowadays, very few businesses think about making products that customers buy once and can use forever.

Whether it is a computer or a phone, it breaks down after a few years, and we are forced to buy a new one even if we do not want to.

To be honest, I think many people believe that, from a business perspective, it is better to make socks that wear out easily so customers will buy them repeatedly rather than spend time and effort making a pair that lasts ten years without tearing.

However, that way of thinking is not good.

It is precisely because we continue producing things this way that the Earth is overflowing with garbage, and in the future the environment may deteriorate to the point where humans can no longer live here.

To protect the Earth’s environment, products that can continue to be used for a long time will be needed throughout the world.

Products made by Japanese craftspeople are exactly that kind of product.

In the near future, such “products that can be used forever” will surely spread throughout the world as highly valuable items.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t28-p1.vietnamese:
This is an article from a magazine.

On the 5th of this month, “Pakkuri Monster,” a highly popular buffet restaurant among young people, opened in Osaka.

The restaurant's distinctive feature is that all the fish used in its dishes are freshly caught that day and shipped directly from Hokkaido.

Furthermore, because the restaurant offers student prices, it is especially popular with younger customers.

The restaurant's headquarters are in Hokkaido. It also opened a branch in Tokyo last year and achieved great success, making the Osaka branch its third location.

At the Tokyo branch, shabu-shabu was especially popular.

However, because the restaurant specializes in adding local specialties to its menu, the Osaka branch offers Osaka specialties in an all-you-can-eat format.

The writer tried interviewing some of the customers.

A man in his 40s said, “I’m from Hokkaido, so it’s wonderful to be able to eat delicious fish here in Osaka.”

A mother who had come with her family said happily, “I have three sons, and cooking meals for them every day is exhausting. Thanks to these low prices, we can eat a lot, so my sons are happy and I get a break too.”

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t29-p1.outline.1.labe: The current state of education about punctuality among Japanese children.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t29-p1.outline.2.labe: Foreign businesspeople's awareness of the value of time
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t29-p1.outline.2.note: Contrary to the earlier stereotype, foreign businesspeople are always punctual because they believe that “time is life,” respect one another’s time, and protect their reputation (evidence for Question 2).
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t29-p1.outline.3.labe: The author's regret over the decline of a good Japanese habit
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t29-p1.outline.3.note: Emphasizes punctuality as a valuable Japanese tradition and expresses regret that many Japanese people today can no longer maintain it (evidence for Question 3).
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t29-p1.vietnamese:
The following essay was written by a Japanese person who has worked in 5 countries.

When I was young, both my parents and my teachers strictly taught me that I must always be punctual.

As a result, I grew up believing that punctuality was simply a matter of course.

However, as the 21st century began, I heard that Japanese children today are not necessarily taught by adults to observe scheduled times.

Naturally, children like that will be unable to be punctual even after they become adults.

Conversely, I feel that among foreigners who were once considered “loose with time,” the number of people who observe scheduled times seems to have increased.

Since joining my current company, I have worked abroad for 20 years, and foreign businesspeople always keep their appointments.

They consider “time to be life.”

Because they do not want their own time to be wasted, they do not do things that waste other people’s time.

They understand very clearly that failing to be punctual causes them to lose the trust of others.

The habit of “being punctual” has long been valued by Japanese people.

Simply by being punctual, one can gain the trust of others, so I feel extremely disappointed to see the increasing number of Japanese people who are unable to do so.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t3-p1.vietnamese:
My son asked me what the difference between vegetables and fruit was, but I could not answer immediately.

We generally have the impression that sweet things are fruit and things that are not sweet are vegetables.

However, I was not sure whether this explanation was correct.

So I tried to find out what the difference was.

The simplest way to distinguish vegetables from fruit is this: things that grow on trees are fruit, and things that do not are vegetables.

But that is not correct.

In fact, many kinds of fruit do not grow on trees.

So what is the correct answer after all?

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t30-p1.vietnamese:
More improvements to make daily life easier for elderly people and people with disabilities have begun to appear in many places than before.

For example, stations and supermarkets always have elevators for people who have difficulty walking.

For people with visual impairments and elderly people, there are also services in which station staff accompany them all the way to the platform.

Measures like these began to appear after a new law was enacted in 2006.

Under this law, places used by many people are required to install at least one elevator and one restroom designated for people with disabilities.

Before then, society had paid little attention to making life more convenient for these people.

However, with 2006 as a turning point, concern for people with disabilities and elderly people grew stronger, and that trend continues today.

People are taking their voices seriously, and places that need improvement are actively being renovated and upgraded.

The government’s attitude of “building a society that is easy for anyone to live in” does not seem to be empty talk at all.

I hope they will continue their efforts toward an even better society in the future.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t31-p1.vietnamese:
When I was in elementary school, many parents opposed their children watching anime.

Their view was: "If you watch anime, your grades at school will get worse."

Some parents even went so far as to say that watching anime would make children stupid.

However, now that I am an adult, I feel that this way of thinking is incorrect.

I have always liked watching anime, and, for example, many foreign loanwords appear in anime.

Therefore, when I began studying English in junior high school, I was able to memorize English vocabulary without any difficulty.

As a result, my English grades were always good.

Also, although I could not play baseball at all, I naturally learned baseball terms and rules by frequently watching baseball anime.

Thanks to this, I became friends with many people who loved baseball, and even while studying abroad in the United States, I was able to make friends with many Americans through baseball.

Anime is an excellent tool for children, helping them learn unfamiliar things with great interest.

In today's world, even knowledge taught at school can be learned through anime.

If you dislike studying from books, you only need to watch anime like this.

Anime absolutely does not make children's minds inferior.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t32-p1.vietnamese:
Even movements that we can perform naturally under normal circumstances may become difficult to perform well when we are tense.

In the case of a baseball player, for example, a player may be able to throw good pitches during practice but, once in a game, become so tense that the body does not move as intended and the player is sometimes unable to throw well.

Stress causes attention to become overly focused on things that we normally do not pay attention to, making it impossible to perform movements as smoothly as usual.

To prevent this from happening during games, baseball players today place great importance on mental training alongside their regular physical practice.

In fact, many athletes have improved their mental condition and significantly enhanced their performance since beginning mental training.

This is not limited to baseball; throughout the world of sports, more and more importance is being placed on mental training.

Some time ago, there were no instructors who understood the importance of mental training, and it was taken for granted that athletes should practice arduously until they gained confidence.

However, that approach is now outdated.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.0.note: The passage describes the growing trend of studying in Taiwan and its major advantages, such as low tuition, proximity to Japan, and the opportunity to study both Chinese and English. This provides the basis for question 1.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.1.labe: The negative side and regrettable consequences at Taiwanese universities
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.1.note: The focus shifts to the negative side: lenient admission standards allowed many people with no Japanese ability to come study abroad and cause problems, leading to reduced enrollment quotas. This supports Question 2.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.2.labe: The author's view of studying abroad without adequate preparation
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.outline.2.note: Although young people are less afraid of going abroad, the author strongly rejects the idea that one can simply go overseas without preparation and automatically become mature. This is the basis for question 3.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t33-p1.vietnamese:
Since 2000, while the number of Japanese people studying abroad is said to have been gradually declining, the number of Japanese people studying at universities in Taiwan has been increasing.

When international students were asked about the appeal of studying in Taiwan, many answered, "Tuition is cheaper than in other countries," "I want to study Chinese," and "It is close to Japan."

Some also answered, "Since many departments at Taiwanese universities teach only in English, it is possible to study both English and Chinese at the same time."

Hearing such accounts makes one admire the high level of awareness among young Japanese people, but there are also negative aspects.

It is said that because the admission requirements for international students at Taiwanese universities are relatively lenient, foreigners can enter them comparatively easily.

As a result, many Japanese people go to Taiwan to study without knowing Chinese.

Such students often cause many problems at their universities, and there have even been reports that one university reduced its quota for Japanese international students.

That is extremely unfortunate.

Compared with the past, young Japanese people have recently become less fearful of foreign countries.

Nevertheless, I cannot agree with the way of thinking that one can simply rush abroad without making any preparations and then mature as a person.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t34-p1.outline.0.note: A friend from high school happens to come to Tokyo on business and calls the author; they arrange to meet for dinner. This passage provides the basis for Question 1.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t34-p1.outline.1.labe: A reunion and impressions of carefree school-day friendship
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t34-p1.outline.1.note: After meeting again for the first time in more than ten years, the two talk enthusiastically, and the author realizes for the first time that school friends are precious friends unburdened by self-interest. This section provides the basis for Question 2.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t34-p1.outline.2.labe: Fresh emotions and the meaning of meeting an old friend again
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t34-p1.outline.2.note: The reunion helps the author recover fresh emotions, feel as though their spirit has returned to student days amid a busy life, and realize the wonderful value of meeting old friends again. This passage provides evidence for Question 3.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t34-p1.vietnamese:
One morning, I received a phone call from a friend from high school.

Apparently, he happened to be in Tokyo on a business trip and remembered that I worked in Tokyo, so he contacted me.

Although it was an unexpected call, I thought it would be nice to meet again after such a long time, so we arranged to have dinner that evening.

That evening, while I was waiting at the restaurant we had chosen, my friend arrived.

Only his figure had become slightly rounder; his face had not changed at all since high school.

Since we had not seen each other for more than 10 years, we talked nonstop until the restaurant closed.

People often say that school friends are precious friends who are not connected by personal gain or loss, and when I talked with him, I felt that for the first time.

Meeting an old friend again after so long gave me a truly strange feeling that day.

In the life of a working person, always swept along by work, I had finally rediscovered fresh emotions after such a long time.

It was as if my soul had returned to the days when I was a high school student.

Perhaps it will be some time before I see him again, but meeting old friends really is a wonderful thing.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t35-p1.outline.1.labe: The role of public bathhouses in bringing families together
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t35-p1.outline.1.note: Many elderly people go with family members to avoid the danger of bathing alone, and the sento serves as a bridge for communication and checking in among family members.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t35-p1.outline.2.note: The author gives reasons for liking sento (the variety of baths, relaxation, and the refreshing feeling of chatting) and concludes that going to a sento occasionally is very beneficial.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t35-p1.vietnamese:
The other day, I went to a public bath for the first time in a long while.

Moreover, since it was well past noon, there were few people there, but I was still surprised to see the place being used by people of all ages, from the elderly to young children.

The older people seemed to quickly become friendly with those they met at the bath. After greeting one another, they would immediately enter the tub together and chat animatedly.

Before going to the public bath, I had assumed that most elderly people went alone, but I was surprised to see that many came with their families.

According to someone at the public bath, the reason is that it is dangerous and worrying for elderly people to bathe alone, so someone in the family always accompanies them.

Apparently, this also gives grandfathers and their sons—who rarely have a chance to talk in daily life—a chance to converse.

Thus, the public bath has become a place where family members check on one another and interact.

I do not usually go very often myself, but I still really like public baths.

That is because you can enjoy various types of baths suited to each season, relax by soaking in hot water, and feel refreshed and invigorated by talking with other people.

Although most households in Japan have their own bathtubs, I feel that occasionally going to a public bath is a wonderful experience.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t36-p1.outline.2.note: The author planned to jog for exercise but developed a sore throat when breathing and could not run for long, especially in cold regions. This provides evidence for Question 3.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t36-p1.outline.3.labe: The strength and resilience of children in cold regions
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t36-p1.outline.3.note: In contrast to the author's difficulties, children carefree run around the park even when the snow is falling and the roads are icy; the author concludes that children are truly strong.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t36-p1.vietnamese:
Sometimes I think that children in cold regions are truly extraordinary.

Because I am not good at handling the cold, when winter comes, I stand in front of the heater after waking up in the morning, and sometimes I cannot move for a while.

But I cannot stay there forever, so I put on several layers of clothing before going outside.

When I go outside, I see several elementary school students walking toward school.

People often say that “children are children of the wind.” Although it is cold, they walk around wearing short sleeves or casually touch the snow with their bare hands, as if they do not feel cold at all.

I cannot stand the cold unless I wear gloves, a hat, and a thick coat, so I feel a little envious.

I also planned to run outdoors in winter to exercise, but whenever I start running, my throat hurts sharply each time I breathe, and I cannot run for long.

This is especially true in very cold regions.

Yet the children continue running and playing energetically around the park, even when it is snowing or the roads are icy.

I truly feel that children are very strong.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t37-p1.vietnamese:
There is a festival called the “Aomori Nebuta Festival,” one of the most famous festivals in Japan.

The festival is said to have begun 400 years ago and is considered one of the three major festivals of the Tohoku region.

Because of the outbreak of the novel coronavirus, the festival was canceled for two consecutive years from 2020, but in August 2022 it was held again for the first time in three years.

Many tourists flocked to the city to see the enormous Nebuta lanterns.

When 17 large Nebuta floats appeared at around 7 p.m., the tourists enthusiastically applauded and took pictures.

Around the Nebuta, dancers called “Haneto” danced while shouting, “Rassera! Rassera!”

One delighted visitor said: “I am a huge fan of the Nebuta Festival and make sure to come every year. I am deeply moved to finally be able to see it again.”

The large figures used in the Aomori Nebuta Festival are about 5 meters tall.

Each Nebuta figure takes up to three months to make, and production costs are said to be around 20 million yen per figure.

Although this is a festival that requires so much time and money, it has connected people in the area for a long time and has been cherished and jointly preserved by the townspeople.

The Nebuta Festival is an important part of Aomori's traditional culture.

The cancellation of the festival in 2020–2021 meant losing opportunities to pass on the importance of traditional culture to younger generations.

However, in the future, I hope that through the Nebuta Festival, young people will grow to love the town where they were born and raised and carry on the festival's traditions.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t38-p1.vietnamese:
I have been a university lecturer for 30 years, and when I compare students today with those of 30 years ago, there is a tremendous difference in their reading habits.

Thirty years ago, students typically read two or three books a month, whereas students today read nothing beyond the books they are required to read for class.

The decline in the amount of reading people do today is extremely serious.

People read for many different reasons, but if I had to name one important benefit of reading, it would be that books allow us to learn about the lives and experiences of their authors.

As long as we have books, we can learn not only from the ideas of contemporary authors but also from the thoughts of authors who have passed away.

By reading, we can transcend time and learn from the experiences and ideas of our predecessors.

However, things are different today.

Schools provide very few opportunities to teach the importance of reading, and both students and teachers believe that studying to achieve high scores on tests is what matters most.

As a result, people today demand study methods that enable them to memorize large amounts of knowledge efficiently, and students come to dislike reading because it takes so much time.

Consequently, more and more young people say that they cannot understand the contents of books.

Although reading is an excellent way to cultivate the mind, I feel that as the number of people unwilling to learn about life continues to increase, so does the number of young people who are anxious about their future path.

If this situation continues, the number of people who lose their way in life will probably increase even further.

What will become of Japan's future if the number of such people continues to grow?

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t39-p1.vietnamese:
I was walking down the street with a friend when a dog approached us from ahead.

Because the dog was wearing a collar, it seemed to be someone's pet.

The collar had the name 「Candy」 written on it in small letters.

However, even after looking around, we could not see anyone who appeared to be its owner.

The dog seemed to be lost. I was a little worried.

I discussed it with my friend, and we decided to take the dog to the police station.

Because we had no leash, we called out 「This way, this way」 as we spent an entire hour leading it to a nearby police station.

While we were explaining the situation to the police, a woman suddenly entered through the door and said, 「That is my dog!」

When the police officer asked, 「Are you absolutely sure this is your dog?」, she immediately replied, 「Yes, there is no mistake. She is my Candy.」

The dog also seemed very happy to see her again and kept wagging its tail. This dog was definitely hers.

The police also looked at the small writing on the collar and confirmed that the dog belonged to her.

According to the owner, the dog had suddenly run away while she was walking it in the park, and she did not know where it had gone.

The owner said to us, 「To thank you for finding Candy, please accept these two tickets,」 then said goodbye and left.

By then, it was already getting late in the afternoon, so we decided to go home as well.

We had originally planned to drink tea and chat at a café that day, but in the end, we had no time left because of the lost dog.

Then, when I happened to look at the tickets the dog's owner had given us, I was surprised to see that they were free coffee vouchers for exactly the café we had planned to visit that day.

「It was wonderful to help someone today. Helping others really makes you feel good. And we even received coffee tickets, so we were truly lucky.」 We returned home feeling extremely happy.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t40-p1.outline.1.labe: The Japanese convention of symbolic partitions and Westerners' reactions
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t40-p1.outline.1.note: Japanese people use noren and shoji to divide rooms. Westerners are surprised and uncomfortable because they feel their private space is not protected. Provides evidence for Questions 2 and 3.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t40-p1.outline.2.labe: Psychological barriers and the advantages of the Japanese way of dividing space
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t40-p1.outline.2.note: Explains how a vague division of space using a 'psychological wall' allows members to sense one another's state while maintaining an appropriate degree of privacy and distance. This supports Question 4.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t40-p1.vietnamese:
In Japanese homes, the usual structure is that when people enter through the entrance (genkan), they first take off their shoes, step up onto a raised floor, and then enter the living room. Western homes, however, do not have anything called a genkan.

In many Western homes, people open the door and walk straight into the living room without taking off their shoes.

While people in Japan distinguish between inside and outside, people in the West do not make such a strong distinction.

Sometimes, people use nothing more than a piece of cloth or paper, such as a noren curtain or shoji sliding door, to divide one room into two spaces and use them as separate areas.

When Westerners see this (①), they feel very surprised.

When wind blows, people can be seen through a noren, and voices from the next room can be heard through shoji.

From their perspective, even if they are family members, they feel uncomfortable if there is no space in the home where they can be alone without being visible to the other members.

From this point of view, the way Japanese people divide space is very vague (②).

Rather than dividing physical space with things such as walls, they divide it with an invisible “psychological wall.”

In this way, family members can sense one another’s situation while maintaining an appropriate sense of distance by dividing the space without intruding too deeply into each other’s privacy.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t41-p1.outline.0.labe: The current state of rapid delivery and consumer psychology
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t41-p1.outline.0.note: Delivery speeds today are astonishingly fast, and consumers now take next-day delivery for granted.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t41-p1.outline.1.labe: Problems and risks facing the transportation industry
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t41-p1.outline.1.note: The downside of rapid delivery: the volume of shipments has surged while drivers are aging and becoming scarce, creating a serious risk that delivery speeds will decline.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t41-p1.outline.3.note: Classify items that do not need urgent delivery so their delivery dates can be postponed, reducing the driver's daily load and protecting the environment.
default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t41-p1.vietnamese:
Nowadays, delivery has become astonishingly fast compared with the past—for example, customers can receive packages “the next day.”

We have also become completely accustomed to this speed, and having online purchases delivered to our homes the following day no longer surprises us.

However, while delivery has become more convenient, the people who deliver all these goods naturally have a very difficult job.

In Japan, as many as 5 billion packages are delivered each year, and that number continues to rise annually.

Furthermore, truck drivers are reportedly getting older, while the number of people working in the field is becoming insufficient.

There is concern that if the volume of goods continues to increase at this rate, delivery speeds will gradually decline sharply, and eventually delivery itself may no longer be possible.

To alleviate this problem even slightly, some moves have begun in the United States to change the mindset that “speed is everything.”

Specifically, customers have been allowed to choose “slow delivery” when placing an order.

Unlike household necessities or food, which people need immediately, items such as clothing and hobby-related goods generally do not need to be received urgently.

In such cases, if buyers choose “slow delivery,” the delivery date can be postponed.

Doing so can reduce the number of packages that need to be delivered in a single day and lessen the burden on drivers.

Furthermore, this option is also expected to benefit the environment.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t42-p1.outline.2.labe: The economic and environmental benefits of sorting waste

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t42-p1.vietnamese:
Do you know where the most detailed waste-sorting rules in Japan are found?

It is in a place called Kamikatsu Town in Tokushima Prefecture.

Although it is a small town with a population of only about 1,400, waste is reportedly sorted into as many as 45 categories.

Its recycling rate is also remarkably high at 81%, making it the town in Japan closest to achieving "zero waste."

So how exactly does Kamikatsu Town sort its waste?

There are no garbage trucks collecting waste in the town. All waste is brought to a single waste-disposal site in the town.

The carefully sorted waste is sold to recycling companies.

Not burning the waste both saves the town's tax money and benefits the environment.

To sort the waste in detail, residents have to wash off dirt stuck to it or dry it, but because they can take out their garbage at any time, some people say this method is actually easier.

When interviewed, one resident said: "After sorting the waste, I feel much lighter. It is enjoyable, and if it is also good for the Earth, I am very happy to do it."

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t5-p1.vietnamese:
This is an email sent by an elementary school to parents.

From: Daiichi Elementary School

Sent: 12:00 p.m., July 25, 2020

Subject: Notice About the School Attendance Day

Dear Parents of Class 2-1,

Thank you for your continued cooperation.

Next Monday, August 2, is a school attendance day.

Students should arrive at school at 8:30 a.m.

After arriving at school, there will be time to listen to instructions from the teachers, followed by a school-wide cleanup.

Please have students come wearing clothes that may get dirty.

Also, since it will be hot, please have them bring a hat and something to drink.

Everything will finish before 11:00 a.m., so they do not need to bring a boxed lunch.

Thank you for your cooperation.

In India, beef and pork are not common food ingredients.

When people talk about eating meat, they usually mean chicken or lamb.

Also, because India has many cars and motorcycles, walking outside is dangerous, so people are said to usually travel by vehicle when they go out.

default.p.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t7-p1.vietnamese:
The moon is beautifully round tonight.

Because it was so beautiful, I suddenly remembered something when I went out to the garden to look at it with my family.

In Japan, people say that the patterns on the moon look like a rabbit, but an international student who stayed with my family last month told me that they look different in other countries.

Apparently, in her country, the patterns on the moon look like a horse.

No matter how I looked at it, I could not see a horse.

However, after she explained it to me, I really could see a horse in it.

This was an extremely interesting discovery for me.

I realized that there is never only one way to perceive something.

default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 個人情報は電話で言うべきではない。
The police notice emphasizes that people must be extremely careful and must not provide financial information, such as credit card or bank account details, to anyone over the phone.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.explanation: The core message of the notice is contained in the sentence: 「電話の相手が誰であっても、クレジットカードや銀行口座の情報は言わないようにしましょう。」(No matter who is on the other end of the phone, let us remember not to disclose credit-card or bank-account information.) Grammatically, 「[noun] + であっても」means “even if it is...” or “no matter what...,” and it combines with 「negative verb + ようにしましょう」to urge listeners to make an effort to prevent a negative situation. In the JLPT, the specific phrase “credit-card and bank-account information” is generalized as “personal information” (個人情報), which corresponds perfectly to the cautionary nuance of「言うべきではない」in choice (c). To avoid losing points, note the distinction from distractor (d): the notice warns against disclosing confidential data during suspicious calls; it does not advise abandoning all telephone communication with banks.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) The passage only discusses criminals impersonating police officers to commit fraud; it does not conclude that there are bad people within the police force.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The text does not say that bank employees never call customers. It warns about criminals pretending to be bank employees in order to steal people's assets.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) The police emphasize that callers must not disclose card or bank-account information, regardless of who is calling. This is equivalent to saying that people should not share personal information over the phone.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t1-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The passage only warns readers not to provide financial information during suspicious calls; it does not advise them to stop all telephone communication with bank employees.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 子供の健康を考えて、毎日のメニューが決められている。
Lunch menus at elementary schools are carefully balanced by nutritionists to provide the necessary nutrients and control salt intake in order to protect children’s health.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.explanation: The passage explains that school lunches are designed for students’ health in the sentence: 「メニューは専門の栄養の先生が毎月決めており、子供が1日に必要な栄養の3分の1、またはそれ以上になるように設定されている。」 (“The menu is determined each month by a specialized nutrition teacher and is designed to provide one-third or more of the nutrients children need each day.”) The school also carefully controls the amount of salt, as shown by 「1日あたりの必要量の3分の1を超えないように作られている」, to compensate for salty meals at home. This shows that every aspect is aimed at supporting the children’s long-term physical condition. The central grammar point is the N3 pattern `V-ru / V-nai + ように`, which expresses a purpose meaning “so that” or “in order to achieve a desired state.” It is often used when the subject adjusts an action to reach a particular result. In this 読解 question, avoid subjective assumptions in options (a) and (c): although parents being pleased or children growing quickly from eating enough nutrients may seem realistic, the author never mentions them, so they must not be inferred as answers.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) The passage only mentions that the school prepares lunch; it does not mention the parents' feelings or happiness.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.why.1: ✓ (b) The lunch menu was planned by a nutritionist to ensure adequate nutrients and limit the amount of salt for the students' health.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The author only states that lunch provides at least one-third of the daily nutritional needs; the passage does not claim that children will grow quickly or develop well.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t10-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The passage says that the dish was seasoned skillfully so that it would not taste bland; it does not recommend adding salt.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 歴史を学ぶと、現在や未来のことがよく分かるようになる。
Studying events from the past helps learners understand the nature of the present and become able to anticipate changes in the future.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.explanation: The key sentence answering the question is the second sentence: 「過去に何が起こったかを知り、それがなぜ起こったのか、当時の人はどう考えていたのかなどを知ることで、今起こっていることの意味や、これから何が起こるのかが予想できるようになるからだ。」 The grammar pattern 「dictionary-form verb + ことで」 expresses means or method ("through doing... / by doing...") and is combined with 「potential form + ようになる」, which describes a change in ability over time ("come to be able to do something"). The complete translation is: "That is because, by learning what happened in the past, why it happened, and what people at the time thought, we become able to understand the meaning of what is happening now and predict what will happen next." To avoid the trap in option (d), distinguish its purpose clearly: the author encourages discussing matters with others to develop the ability to consider them from various perspectives (色々な角度から物事が考えられる), not to gain a deeper understanding of history.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) The author does not say that merely listening to others prevents one from understanding the importance of history; the author only recommends exchanging opinions to broaden one's perspective.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.why.1: ✓ (b) The author points out that learning about the past helps us explain what is happening now and predict the future.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The passage recommends developing this way of studying from a young age, which is the complete opposite of the idea that one should wait until entering the workforce to learn it.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t11-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) Communicating with others is intended to develop a multifaceted perspective on things, not to gain a deeper understanding of history.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t12-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) お店の人が高齢になったから
Kobayashi Shoten decided to close at the end of next month because the shop owner has become too old to continue running the business.
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t12-q1.explanation: The direct evidence is in the third sentence of the passage: 「しかし、店主がこれ以上営業を続けるのが難しい歳となり、来月末で営業を終了することに致しました。」 (However, the owner has reached an age at which it is difficult to continue operating the business, so we have decided to close at the end of next month.) The key grammar point is 「[V-る + のが難しい] + 歳となり」, combining 「〜のが難しい」, which says that carrying out an action has become difficult, with an age noun and 「となる」, a formal connective form of となって expressing a transition into a state. This is a tactful, formal announcement equivalent to 「高齢になった」 (“has become elderly”). The structure 「〜ことに致しました」 (V-る + ことにいたしました) is the formal humble form of 「〜ことにしました」 and emphasizes that the store's decision to close directly resulted from the owner's age. To avoid being misled by choices (a) and (b), pay attention to the time context in 「〜ことが何度もありました」: economic downturns and the construction of shopping malls were past difficulties the shop had faced and overcome, not the reason for closing next month.

default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t13-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) 水道管工事は平日の日中に行われる。
According to the notice, the water-pipe repair work will take place on Wednesday, September 10 (a weekday, 平日), from 10:00 to 17:00 (during the daytime, 日中).
default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t13-q1.explanation: The original notice states: 「当マンションは9月10日（水）の10時から17時の間、水道管工事のため、断水になります。」 ("Water service in our apartment building will be suspended from 10:00 to 17:00 on Wednesday, September 10, because of water-pipe construction.") The key skill is recognizing paraphrases in JLPT N3 questions: Wednesday (水曜日) is generalized as a weekday (平日, へいじつ, Monday through Friday, as opposed to holidays), and 10:00–17:00 is understood as daytime (日中, にっちゅう, as opposed to nighttime, 夜間). Grammatically, the notice uses the respectful pattern 「ご + Sino-Japanese noun + になる」 in the negative potential form 「ご使用になれません」 (equivalent to 使うことができません), as well as the polite humble potential expression 「ご利用いただけます」 (equivalent to 利用できます). These forms are common in public notices and service instructions, showing respect for residents and customers. In particular, 「なお、1階の共同トイレはご利用いただけます。」 means: "Please note that the shared restroom on the first floor remains available." To avoid distractors such as (b), pay attention to 「なお」, which adds an exception or relaxed rule contrasting with the general prohibition stated immediately before.

default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t13-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) During the water shutdown, washing clothes at home is also suspended and cannot be done, along with using the shower and toilet (洗濯、シャワー、トイレはご使用になれません).

default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t14-q1.verdict:

default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t16-q1.verdict:

In a workplace context, it politely expresses a request for someone to complete an action in advance as preparation for subsequent work. The expression「目を通す」means to look over or check a document, and it combines with the reported-speech forms「〜そうです / 〜とのことです」, which follow the plain form 普通形, to convey a third party's request politely. An important strategy for reading-comprehension note questions (伝言メモ) is to identify the subject of each action precisely: Yamada is the person who revised the material (今朝、資料を一部変更した), not Mr. Chin. Together with the earlier concern about climate change (「これも地球温暖化と関係があるのでしょうか」), this shows that the author fears global environmental deterioration may erode this valuable feature of Japan. Be careful not to overinterpret choice (b): the author raises a question rather than making an absolute prediction about the future (来年以降はもう...できなくなりそう). Therefore, the moderate possibility expressed by 「かもしれない」 in choice (c) is the correct answer.

Combined with the prefix 不- and the negative progressive form 〜ていない, the double-negative structure 不健康な体をしていない subtly emphasizes that most Vietnamese people have well-balanced, healthy physiques. The complete meaning of sentence (d) is: "The reason there are many Vietnamese people who do not have unhealthy bodies is that they regularly eat vegetables." The direct evidence is quoted from the passage: 「言われてみると、ベトナムに行った時に太っている人をほとんど見かけませんでしたが、もしかするとその理由はベトナム料理にあるのかもしれません。」 together with the habit 「普段から野菜を多く食べる習慣があります。」 An important N3 distinction is to recognize the paraphrase between not seeing many overweight people and not having unhealthy physiques, while rejecting traps such as (a) and (c), which use 「男女関係なく」to add unsupported claims about appearance or concerns about weight.

The key N3 grammar is V-dict + 上で, which takes the dictionary form and indicates a prerequisite or an essential condition within a process, often combined with expressions of necessity such as 「絶対に必要だ」. By contrasting sleep with the risk of being attacked, the author emphasizes that restoring physical condition is the ultimate way for animals to protect their bodies and lives (自分の体を守るため). To avoid the trap in choice (c), 疲れをとるため, remember the N3 reading strategy: do not choose an answer merely because it repeats a word from the passage, such as 疲れた. Focus on the author's central purpose.

Since the rescheduled flight the next morning does not suit Mr. Hayashi’s wish to arrive early, he should call the designated customer-service number and ask whether there are any alternative flights.

Since Mr. Hayashi wants to arrive in Los Angeles as soon as possible (少しでも早くロサンゼルスに着きたい), a flight delayed by 19 hours is an inconvenient situation (ご都合が悪い). default.q.tw6kai_dokkai_n3-t21-q1.verdict:

Because the highway bus was canceled and the ticket fare was refunded at the counter, passengers can switch to another means of transportation.
